title: How to Handle a Question You Do Not Know
interviewAnswer: Do not bluff. State what you know, identify the uncertain part, reason from first principles, and describe how you would verify it. A structured partial answer is usually stronger than confident guessing.
keyPoints: Ask one clarifying question only when necessary
Never invent metrics or implementation details
why: Interviewers do not expect perfect recall, but they do evaluate honesty, composure and whether you can reason from fundamentals when knowledge is incomplete.
intuition: Separate “I do not remember the exact fact” from “I have no idea.” State the boundary, explain what you do know, and reason forward without inventing details.
deepDive: A useful pattern is: clarify the question → state the known part → identify the uncertain part → reason from first principles → suggest how you would verify it. If the interviewer corrects you, incorporate the correction rather than defending a guess. For implementation questions, describe a debugging or research plan. For resume claims, never fabricate details you cannot defend.
workedExample: “I have not used SageMaker professionally, so I would not claim hands-on depth. I have built ADF/SQL ETL pipelines and understand ingestion, orchestration, monitoring and failure recovery; I would map those concepts to the AWS services and verify the service-specific behavior in the docs.”
commonMistakes: Bluffing with confident but false terminology.
Saying only “I don’t know” when you can still reason usefully.
Talking indefinitely instead of clearly stating the uncertainty.
followUps: Which part are you confident about?
How would you verify your assumption?
Can you derive the answer from a simpler case?
production: The same behavior matters in engineering: acknowledge uncertainty, make assumptions explicit, test them cheaply, and use logs/docs/experiments instead of guessing in production.
